finding.claim: DELETE /reports/:id performs the removal without enforcing authorization because authorize() is called without await, so its rejection is discarded.
finding.source: Any request to DELETE /reports/:id; req.user is taken from req.session.user (server.js:5), and no grant is required for the removal to proceed.

trace.note: authorize() called without await; returns a promise, so the 403 throw at line 14 is an unhandled rejection
remove executes regardless of authorization outcome

finding.guards_checked: authorize() (server.js:9-16) computes the correct decision but its result is discarded; no route-level middleware guards this route. On denial, Node 15+ unhandled-rejection default may crash the process, racing the removal. Crash behavior is from Node semantics; the repro was denied sandbox permission and was not executed.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() (server.js:9-16) throws on denial, but the call at server.js:20 has no await and its returned promise is discarded, so the throw never reaches the handler. No route-level middleware guards DELETE /reports/:id (server.js:4-7 only sets req.user from req.session.user, and server.js:18 registers no guard). The PUT route at server.js:27 uses await and is correctly guarded, which makes the DELETE omission an inconsistency rather than an intentional design.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: authorize() at server.js:9-16 is async and throws on denial, but server.js:20 calls it without await, so db.reports.remove at server.js:21 runs regardless of the grant check. The attacker needs only a session with a user (server.js:5), i.e. an authenticated low-privilege user, and no effective control blocks it.

finding.claim: Denied or missing-resource PUT requests produce an unhandled promise rejection that can crash the process on Express 4 (DoS), though the write itself is blocked.
finding.source: PUT /reports/:id where the caller lacks write, the report does not exist (null), or req.user is undefined.
finding.sink: Unhandled rejection from the async Express handler; process termination.

trace.note: resource.id or user.id throws TypeError when report or user is missing

finding.guards_checked: The await on line 27 correctly blocks the update, so this is DoS, not authz bypass. Express 5 would route the rejection to the error handler. No package.json present, so Express version is unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none. No try/catch or error-handling middleware in server.js; the `await authorize(...)` at server.js:27 does block the write (so this is not an authz bypass), but it does not catch the rejection. The only other guard, the 403 throw at server.js:14, is itself the rejection source.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: a null report or undefined req.user makes `resource.id` / `user.id` throw at server.js:10, the 403 is thrown at server.js:14, and the async handler at server.js:25-30 has no catch, so the rejection is unhandled. Whether that crashes the process depends on the Express version, which cannot be determined because no package.json exists in the directory (the Glob for package.json returned nothing), and on Node's unhandled-rejection mode (default crash on Node 15+), so the DoS claim cannot be confirmed from the code available.

finding.claim: Mass assignment: the entire request body is passed to db.reports.update, allowing a caller with write on one report to modify any field the DB layer accepts.
finding.source: req.body parsed by express.json() (server.js:3); no field allowlist.

trace.note: authorize checks write on the report

finding.guards_checked: authorize() gates on action and resource only, not on which fields change. Impact depends on the db schema, which is not in the repo. Confidence medium.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at server.js:9-16 is awaited at server.js:27 and throws a 403 on missing "write" grant, so unauthorized callers never reach the update at server.js:28. No field allowlist exists between req.body (server.js:3, 28) and the sink. The db.reports.update implementation is not in the repo, so any schema-level filtering there cannot be checked.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: express.json() at server.js:3 feeds req.body unfiltered into db.reports.update at server.js:28, and the awaited authorize() at server.js:27 correctly gates on "write". Whether this is exploitable depends on which fields db.reports.update accepts and whether a write-granted user gains anything beyond editing content (e.g. owner or grant fields), and that schema is not in the repo, so the impact cannot be decided from the code available.

finding.claim: Authentication and CSRF posture cannot be verified: req.session is read without any session middleware in this file, and state-changing routes have no CSRF protection in-file.
finding.source: Unauthenticated or cookie-bearing requests to any route.
finding.sink: req.session.user read at server.js:5 (throws TypeError if req.session is undefined, causing 500 on every request); state-changing DELETE/PUT routes.
finding.guards_checked: No session middleware or CSRF protection is defined in this file; configuration may exist elsewhere and is out of scope.

verdict.guard_found: none in server.js: no session middleware is registered (only express.json() at line 3 and the req.session reader at lines 4-7), and no CSRF protection exists; the rest of the app (where session middleware could live) is not in the directory.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (server.js:5 reads req.session.user with no session middleware in this file), but whether that is a vulnerability or a crash depends on session and CSRF setup outside server.js, which is not in the directory, so the claim cannot be confirmed or refuted from the code available. The file does show a separate real bug the candidate missed: server.js:20 calls authorize() without await, so a failed check becomes an unhandled rejection and the DELETE at line 21 still runs.

finding.claim: Server binds to all interfaces without TLS or host restriction.
finding.guards_checked: None; exposure rather than a direct vulnerability. Low severity.

verdict.guard_found: none. server.js:32 is `app.listen(3003);` with no host argument, so Node binds all interfaces. Nothing in server.js restricts the host or adds TLS. Express is plain HTTP (server.js:1-2). Any upstream firewall, proxy, or container network setting lives outside this directory and was not checked.
verdict.reason: server.js:32 calls app.listen(3003) without a host, so the server binds all interfaces, and no code in server.js (lines 1-32) restricts the host or adds TLS. Whether this is reachable from outside depends on the deployment's network controls, which are outside this directory. The finding is a low-severity exposure, not a direct exploit.
